- ‌**lada** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Lada.

mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Lada ‌place ​love, beauty, ​spring ​at ​the center ​of ‌a ​living mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Lada ‌appears ​in slavic ‌tradition ​as ​love, beauty, ​spring. ​The ​name's meaning, ‌"Lady, ​order", shapes ‌the ​narratives ‌told about ​this ‌figure.

### ​Worship and ‌Memory ​(Cult)

​Devotees and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ‌Lada ​in ​ritual, text, ‌and ​iconography, ​ensuring the ‌name ​survived ​into the ‌modern ​scholarly record.

‌The ​myths ​of Lada ​survive ​in ‌fragments, summaries, ‌and ​later ‌retellings. Each ​version ​reflects the ‌interests ‌of ‌its tellers ‌— ​poets, ‌priests, philosophers, ​and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Lada ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Lada ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Slavic ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Lada, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​love ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Lada** ​(*lada*) — ‌Love, Beauty, ‌Spring ​· Lady, ​order ​— belongs ​to the ​Slavic ‌tradition, where ​it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"Love, Beauty, ​Spring". The ‌name ​means "Lady, ​order"[^1].

**Lada** ​is ​the Slavic ​goddess ‌of love, ​harmony, and ‌spring ​— or ‌perhaps a ​folk-song ‌cry that ​the ‌chroniclers turned ​into a ​goddess. ‌Every written ‌source naming ‌her ​is late: ​medieval ‌glosses, a ​Renaissance school ​play, ‌and spring ​refrains sung ​on ‌Jurjevo (St ​George's ‌Day). Her ​divine status ​is ​debated; her ​presence in ‌the ‌song tradition ​is ‌not.[^2]

PuniCodex ​records the ​canonical ‌scholarly spelling ‌**Lada** and ‌serves ‌its temple ​at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/lada/). ​The displayed ​form ​is ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description ​computed from ​the ‌displayed form ​itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ‌*lada* contains ​the ‌same letters: ​no ‌recovered diacritics ​or special ‌encoding ‌is claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
No ​indigenous ‌written attestation ‌survives ​for ​this ​name; **Lada** ​is ​a ‌scholarly ​transliteration of ​the ‌reconstructed ​spoken ‌form. ​Etymologically the ‌name ​means ​"Lady, ​order"[^1].

The ​canonical ​spelling ‌**Lada** ​matches the ‌conventional ​scholarly ‌romanization. ​The plain ‌ASCII ​form ‌*lada* ​contains the ​same ‌letters, ‌so ‌no ​lost diacritics ​or ‌encoding ​transition ​is claimed. ‌The ​editorial ​work ‌is to ​fix ‌one ​reviewed ​reference spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization ‌and ‌provenance, and ​keep ‌the ​original ​evidence ‌visible. The ‌displayed ‌form ‌is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a ​description ​computed ​from the ‌displayed ​form ​itself.

​The letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- ​**l** ​→ **L** ‌— ​Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**a** ‌→ **a** ​— ‌Same
- ‌**d** ​→ **d** ​— ​Same
- ​**a** ‌→ **a** ‌— ​Same

meditation.body: Most ​goddesses in ‌this ‌lexicon were ​carved, inscribed, ​or ​sung into ​epics; ​Lada survives ‌in the ​one ​medium memory ‌never ​loses — ‌the chorus. ​Hers ‌is a ​strange ​immortality: the ​sources that ​name ​her are ‌late, ​contradictory, and ‌partly ​fraudulent, yet ‌the refrain ​they ‌record is ​older ‌than any ​of them, ​still ‌sung on ‌a ‌Balkan hillside ​every May. ​The ‌lesson she ​teaches ​is about ‌evidence itself. ​A ​word repeated ‌at ​weddings and ‌spring ​fires for ​a thousand ​years ​need not ‌have ‌been a ​god to ‌be ​holy; ritual ​can ‌consecrate a ‌syllable. To ‌study ‌Lada is ​to ‌watch scholarship ​and devotion ​negotiate: ​the scholar ‌asks ​'goddess or ​refrain?', ​the grandmother ‌answers 'Lado!' ​— ​and both ​are ‌keeping the ​tradition alive, ‌which ​may be ‌what ​tradition is. ‌Her temple, ‌honestly ​built, is ​a ​round dance ​with no ‌image ‌at its ​center.[^1]
